flagship.headline: Rolling Stones show at Royal Albert Hall ends in a riot
flagship.summary_line_1: The Rolling Stones opened their 1966 UK tour at London's Royal Albert Hall on September 23, 1966, with Ike & Tina Turner and the Yardbirds opening, according to the venue's own account of the night.
flagship.summary_line_2: Fans rushed the stage during the opening notes of Paint It, Black and broke through the barricades, and the chaos was captured on film and later used in the band's promotional video for Have You Seen Your Mother, Baby.

events.headline: The Paul is Dead rumor breaks nationally
events.summary_line_1: Northern Illinois University's student newspaper, the Northern Star, published a story on September 23, 1969, claiming Paul McCartney had died in a 1966 car crash and been secretly replaced, a claim later proven false.
events.summary_line_2: Radio DJs and fans raced to find clues in songs like Strawberry Fields Forever, and within weeks the rumor had gone international before McCartney himself put it to rest.

events.headline: The Beatles begin recording Happiness Is a Warm Gun
events.summary_line_1: The Beatles gathered in Studio Two at EMI Studios on September 23, 1968, for a 7pm to 3am session that opened work on John Lennon's Happiness Is a Warm Gun, running through 45 takes of the rhythm track, according to the Beatles Bible's session log.
events.summary_line_2: Lennon had stitched the song together from three unfinished fragments, and the band spent two more sessions splicing takes before finishing the White Album track before dawn on September 26.

events.headline: The Box Tops hit No. 1 with The Letter
events.summary_line_1: The Box Tops' debut single The Letter reached number one on the Billboard Hot 100 on September 23, 1967, driven by sixteen-year-old Alex Chilton's raspy lead vocal.
events.summary_line_2: Producer Dan Penn cut the track at American Sound Studio in Memphis, and the two-minute single held the top spot for four weeks and went on to sell more than four million copies.

events.headline: The Rolling Stones release Have You Seen Your Mother, Baby
events.summary_line_1: Decca and London Records released the Rolling Stones' single Have You Seen Your Mother, Baby, Standing in the Shadow? simultaneously in the UK and US on September 23, 1966, backed with Who's Driving My Plane.
events.summary_line_2: Mike Leander's brass arrangement pushed the band toward a harder, more theatrical sound, and the single reached number five in Britain while cracking the American top ten for the Rolling Stones.

events.headline: The Walker Brothers hit UK No. 1 with Make It Easy on Yourself
events.summary_line_1: The Walker Brothers reached number one on the UK Singles Chart with their cover of Make It Easy on Yourself on September 23, 1965, according to the Official Charts Company, their first chart-topper as a trio.
events.summary_line_2: The Burt Bacharach and Hal David song gave the Southern California transplants their breakthrough overseas, and its orchestral heartbreak became a blueprint the group leaned on for the rest of the decade.

events.headline: Lincoln Center opens with Bernstein and a new Copland premiere
events.summary_line_1: Leonard Bernstein conducted the New York Philharmonic's inaugural concert at Philharmonic Hall on September 23, 1962, giving the world premiere of Aaron Copland's Connotations as the centerpiece of Lincoln Center's opening night, according to the New York Philharmonic's own archives.
events.summary_line_2: The concert reached a national CBS television audience, and Copland's stark, twelve-tone score shocked listeners expecting something closer to Appalachian Spring, one of classical music's boldest opening-night gambles.

events.headline: The Real Ambassadors premieres at Monterey with Louis Armstrong
events.summary_line_1: Dave and Iola Brubeck's jazz musical The Real Ambassadors had its only full live performance at the Monterey Jazz Festival on September 23, 1962, starring Louis Armstrong alongside Carmen McRae and the trio Lambert, Hendricks & Ross, according to KQED.
events.summary_line_2: The show used satire and vocal jazz to confront segregation and Cold War-era cultural diplomacy, carrying the same spirit Columbia had captured in the studio the year before for jazz and easy listening audiences.

events.headline: Dizzy Gillespie plays A Musical Safari at Monterey
events.summary_line_1: Dizzy Gillespie led his quintet through a set he introduced as A Musical Safari at the Monterey Jazz Festival on September 23, 1961, with Argentine pianist Lalo Schifrin folding bossa nova into the group's bebop foundation.
events.summary_line_2: The performance later surfaced as a live album, and it remains one of the clearest documents of how deeply Brazilian rhythm reshaped American jazz and easy listening during the early 1960s.
